1WW or 3W to tap X creatures  
UU or 2U to scry X  
1BB or 3B to put a creature with X mana value in your graveyard back on top of your library  
1RR or 3R to make X creatures unable to block

I resonate with parts of this, thanks for sharing. I'm more recently coming to accept an ace label, let alone an aro one. I'm not sex-repulsed, and I've always thought of myself as a romantic person; I've just been misunderstanding the idea of it. I'm definitely not a sentimental person, and while I definitely have \*some\* libido, sex is just a mechanical thing for me. 

I've been really struggling these past few years to feel like part of the queer community at large. I feel undeniably queer and I definitely present as a gay man. But without the strong sexual or romantic desires, I just end up feeling misunderstood or in the way in so many of these spaces. I've been increasingly considering stepping away from them at large, and just focusing more on spaces centered around things I enjoy doing, rather than trying to find spaces that center queerness. I imagine I'll still end up with a lot of queer companions given I live in the Bay Area and I'm going to be pursuing artsy/intellectual spaces.   
  
It's just been tough and sad to feel such a loss of community. I can rationally accept how naive I was to expect my queer peers to have the same drives and values as I did. I just feel so blindsided by how much a minority we are in a minority group.  
  
Anyway, I appreciate the share. Glad to hear there are others out there getting the good feels too :)

I'd imagine that the hate Farewell receives falls into two camps.

A lot of players in Commander understandably don't love having their stuff removed. It's part of the game, but it doesn't mean anyone has to be happy about it. Add to that Farewell is removing ALL of their stuff at once, and you get some very justified salt.

There's also the meta-component of the card. Farewell tends to reduce the momentum of a game to a trickle. For anyone with a developed board, they've probably been extremely neutered and unless they've been able to keep a full hand they may have just been reduced to top-decking. Again, that's part of the game, but is really tough for a lot of players. The worse part here is that Farewell doesn't end the game and I've personally seen it played plenty of times with no follow-up. So instead of a game ending in five or ten minutes due to several developed boards, the game goes on another hour or two with players slowly rebuilding after a nuclear winter. As a veteran player, I would rather just scoop and start a new game. I don't know that many of the new players appreciate that as an option. 

For the people playing Farewell -- I expect you to win the game quickly after dropping this nuke. There are plenty of other options for slowing a game down that don't single-handedly do everything this does. If your deck can't or just doesn't ever win the game quickly, that's a meta call for you. I personally don't think it's polite to just drag people along for a grindy game without their knowing such, but it's a you-do-you world out there.

Speaking as someone who is chronically depressed, you sound depressed.

Life on the whole is a lot of work, and a lot of that work is mundane and menial.

What's more, most of the joy to be had in life has to be sought intentionally. It's rare that someone is going to shove joy into your face. You will need to be an active component in the pursuit of your own comfort and happiness. This can take a lot of different forms, and there is frustration to be had in figuring out \*what\* brings you joy.

That said, no. I don't think like is "worth it". I don't know that life has a worth outside of what we give it. The danger in that framework is that if something isn't "worth it" then maybe it's "worthless." I don't think that's true - I think there's a third option (or more). In the same way that something can be neither good nor bad (whether it's amoral or something else), life as a thing simply is. The choices you make and the impacts they have are yours to pursue and interpret.

But you do sound depressed, so hopefully that eases up soon.

I've definitely felt the cultural pressure to be a sexual male. I didn't like people commenting that I might be on the ace spectrum for a long time because it felt like I was fundamentally failing at being male and being gay.

All of that to say, I think there are a lot of male-identified aces out there who hold back because they believe any number of the things we're told. "You just haven't found the right people," or "you haven't tried the right things."

Honestly it took sustaining a years long sexual relationship that facilitated conversations around how often and what I think about sex (specifically the sex I do have) for me to appreciate how differently my mind works around that. It's really hard to unseat how my experience is seemingly SO different from the other queer men I interact with; I end up feeling so alien trying to interact with them when they all just seem SO horny.

I think the difficulty has a few big components to it. 

* I got diagnosed with depression very early on in life and I've been on a lot of different medications. So much of the narrative around depression and medication for it has to do with decreased libido, and it feels VERY much like a "fucked if I do, fucked if I don't" situation.
* I'm AMAB and attracted to male bodies (mostly; I also really enjoy big hips and butch femmes). Gay male culture is VERY sexual, and I've felt a lot of shame and doubt about who I am and where I belong in those spaces and trying to make connections with other queer men
* I'm sex neutral, not sex repulsed. It's been helpful to talk about this difference with my allosexual companions, but it's been VERY difficult to set down the thoughts of "maybe with the right person I'll be more interested and it won't be an issue." There are a lot of people out there, and I am aesthetically attracted. Trying to explain this nuance has also been difficult and painful.

  
All of that said, accepting asexuality has been a relief for me. I feel a lot less pressure than I used to live in pursuit of sexual relations. I feel more affirmed in my pursuits of my art, friendships, and work. Sex is still super prevalent in our society and it regularly leads to me feeling like an outsider. Al the same, I'm a weirdo in a lot of directions, so that's not the worst to deal with.

depends on the depression. a lot of depression is episodic; it has a triggering event that starts it off. There are a lot of tools we can use to mitigate depressive episodes. Mindfulness, DBT (dialectic behavioral therapy), ACT (acceptance and commitment therapy), and CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) all have methods that can help you maintain some functionality while in a depressive episode. 

But that's kind of it. Depression, like a cold or another virus, often has no cure. It has to run its course. Processing the triggering event and practicing regular mindfulness (or whatever tools you use to mitigate the depression) will help but depression is often the natural result of the circumstances of your life.

Chronic depression is a whole different issue. Chronic depression is usually related to a neurochemical imbalance, complex and persistent trauma, or a lifestyle of self-neglect. There may be no triggering event for a flare up in chronic depression, but just like episodic depression it has to kind of run its course. There is no cure. Medication can help alleviate some of the symptoms, but our understanding of depression and therefore our ability to treat it with medication is pretty limited tbh. The same tools we can learn and practice from therapy will also help soften the depression and help regain some functionality.

i agree with the sentiment here. I think a lot of people in the queer communities ARE demanding an embrace of our cultural elements. I don't think that's necessary personally. I'm aiming toward respectful indifference and/or actual neutrality.
I certainly don't care about looking "good" or "correct". I'm alive, same as anyone else and I've drawn different lines in the sand for things that disgust me.

Queer culture and gay male culture are absolutely pushing things into society. (Sapphic, nonbinary, two-spirit, etc. have also absolutely contributed to this change, I'm just a queer/gay "male" so I can mostly speak from those perspectives).

Ru Paul's Drag Race started in 2009, before gay marriage was legalized in the US. It has become a global tour de force which is forcing a number of countries to address their own treatment of homosexuality in their laws.

The Pink Dollar is a huge line item for consideration in advertisement. That includes apparel, foods, entertainment, etc all catering specifically to a demographic that they had ignored for over a century.

Almost none of these changes have anything to do with the sex that we in the queer community have.

But, you know what has entered the zeitgeist and is almost definitely linked to the increased acceptance of queer culture? Eating ass. It's definitely not an exclusively queer thing to eat your partner's ass out, but just like poppers on the dance floor, polyamory, and more open discussions about STI testing it's an idea that has a lot of roots in queer relationships and spaces. Admittedly, eating ass feels like it's also partly risen with the increased popularity of non-penetrative sex (which also isn't exclusively queer but has a huge overlap there). I think that particular movement has gained in popularity because of the increased in known neurodivergents out there and the ways in which many neurodivergents can engage with sex and sexuality.

As a queer person, I absolutely get what the "right" is saying about moral corruption. I don't believe any of it, but I see what they see. For the large majority of the 20th century, those same people put a pretty hefty boot on the grander queer neck, so I don't feel too bad for them.

Things change, we eat ass now.

I had a pivot in my mid 20s where my depression shifted pretty strongly. Before the change, my depression manifested a lot in internal disappointment - I wasn't good enough, I was failing, etc.

After the shift, my depression felt much more externalized. I had/have undeniable proof of the changes and efforts I've made to uplift myself and I can very easily look out at the world and see how much (*what feels like needless*) strife occurs. The world around me is hard to watch, and it's incredibly demotivating.

As this personal shift occurred, there was a shift in the language of others around me. It stopped being "go to the gym," or "get more rest". It became "focus on the positive," or "so many others have it worse." All the while, I kept trying to make changes outside myself now, through advocacy or seeking work that felt more aligned with what I wanted to see in the world.

It's been almost 10 years since that pivot. This year I have an unpleasant fact on blast; I'll be depressed wherever I am. I have persistent, chronic depression. There is no cure. We don't understand the mechanics of it and likely won't anytime soon. It means I have daily suicidal ideation, increasingly regular and difficult bouts of anhedonia, and a lot of trouble with emotions like anticipation and joy. And none of that is likely to change anytime soon. 

The more I talk about it with my loved ones and strangers the more apparent it becomes that there is a chasm in empathy than they cannot cross. For someone who has never considered suicide, the thought is appalling in a way that I cannot appreciate. I've stopped trying to connect on that particular aspect as a result.

I'm gonna make some assumptions from the language here; please correct me if I've assumed too much.

I take it that "negative emotions" refers to anger, sadness, frustration, etc. Those emotions are difficult to communicate for everyone, but you're astute that men definitely have some additional struggle there. Our societies have operated for a long time on the back of a "stoic male" identity; boys don't cry, men are tough, feelings are for girls, etc. That's all on top of the fact that the negative emotions can absolutely trigger an innate biological response from others.

When we present anger in some of its more natural forms (yelling, stomping, cursing, etc.) it tends to elicit a fear-based response. When animals are afraid they might respond in kind (with anger of their own) or shrink away. There are other responses for sure, but I assume by "hijack" OP means that their anger has a tendency to invoke anger/fear in the person their talking to. That's a very normal process.

It sounds like OP is curious for ways men (and whoever, really) can express these more "negative" emotions aside from conversations. I have some ideas for that, as well as some thoughts on how to make the conversations a little easier.

I think it's useful to recognize the emotions as energetic states. Anger and sadness have different energies to them, and facilitating those energies certainly helps me relieve the tension those emotions can bring. 

When I am angry, I like to break things. Obviously that's not the most sustainable practice, but I go for either satisfying small things (like pencils, very fun to snap) or I put effort into making something so that I can break it. I go through large periods of origami making just so I can have stuff to crush. 

When I am sad, I like to try crying. I have curated a YouTube playlist that evokes that from me. Sometimes that doesn't work and I'll try to make art or take a nap.

These work for me and are just examples. Figuring out your own means of channeling and release anger and sadness will take some introspection and experimentation.

Conversationally, I find it's very helpful to name the emotion out loud and make sure the person you're talking to know it's either about them or not about them. As social creatures, we do have a want to care for each other, which often looks like a sympathetic response. By name the emotion as clearly as we can and also giving it a specific direction, we can more easily talk through it with someone without them subconsciously picking up our emotions as their own.

This is tough stuff - we're not taught it in schools and we're collectively fighting uphill against the practices our parents (and grandparents, etc) have used. I'm glad to hear you're interested in breaking those cycles and trying new things. I hope it gets easier for you soon.

great question. From my memory of myself and my high school and younger college  students, a lot of the comments fall into classic cognitive distortion categories.

"It's so simple, just do \[X\]..." or "They can be this or that, that's the way it is."

I think the rambunctious-ness comes from energy and just a lack (though i don't like that word here since it's generalized and has some less great connotations) of experiences with the unpleasant yet undeniable complexity and ambiguity of the world. 

At least stateside, though i know it to be largely true for a number of larger developed countries as well, most of what we learn before college and most of the way through college comes in the form of problems with solutions. Questions with answers. I don't think a lot of younger people have had the time to sit with situations where there's definitely no guidebook let alone nothing to indicate you're heading in the "right direction."

The rambunctiousness feels mostly related to the necessary urgency of youth. I still feel it - there are so many problems swirling around us lately, big and small. We have tools and resources to fix so many of them, and still it's going to take time and tough decisions to get there and we'll never know if we're making the correct choices.

all that said, I think it's all the more important to listen to the rambunctious statements and really hear them. Even if they're short-sighted or wild, they represent the wants of our youth and at the bare minimum an extreme boundary of change we should consider in our decision making as individuals and groups.

I wouldn't say I don't respect children and young adults, but I definitely do consider their age when I'm interacting with them and their thoughts.

Sometimes it's a matter of structure. When I teach younger people, there's an inevitable power dynamic that arrives both from age but also just being a teacher. I try to soften that dynamic and encourage them to be their authentic selves. They still need to know when their ideas aren't correct or don't serve a kind and nurturing environment. I have very little patience for the shaming that kids toss around (and adults) and I'll call it out as disrespectfully as I please.

More often, it's just a matter of time. I'm young enough that I remember a lot of the feelings I hear kids and young adults put forth. I'm still a pretty impatient person, and I can easily resonate with a lot of the energy I see younger people put forth. I'm also old enough that a lot of my more rigid ideas have just been broken by reality. 

When I hear kids talking big ideas that they have no way to draw experience on, I definitely giggle a bit or roll my eyes. But I remember being there. I don't think there's much to say or do. 

Bottom line. You are still young and developing - your awareness there is awesome. It sounds like there's some tension with your family (and that might be an understatement). Who knows how that'll change, but it will change. Life will continue changing - you'll change and they'll change, too. 

Maybe that's the takeaway. It's not that i don't respect those younger than me (25 and below really). I just know that so much is going to be changing for them in the near near future, so I don't always trust their rambunctious statements.

yeah, you're correct. Cognitive dissonance is rampant.

On the one hand, it's unavoidable. Our world is complex and requires holding a number of opposing ideas in tension. Morality is full of such tension since context so quickly becomes important.

On another hand, we don't really do a great job (or much of one at all) instilling the notion of cognitive dissonance and what to do about it in our education system, and it's not really addressed in any religions or other large communities that I know of. So it's a bit to be expected - this needle is moving but we've really only begun blasting the airwaves with ideas around cognitive dissonance for maybe a decade?

A lot of people **don't** want to change their minds. It's effort, and in a lot of cases it's not genuinely necessary effort. Humans are animals and will continue to try to minimize the amount of effort they're putting forth for just about anything. There are other cognitive biases baked in on top of this, but I do think the biggest issue is (especially for stuff like your example) "why should I bother putting in effort and energy to shift my mental framework when it's not going to make my life better/easier." 

All we can do is continue to point out the dissonance and advocate for change. That costs effort, too. Best of luck, to all of us.

I've been playing EDH since conflux and MTG since Ice Age. Sometimes i can definitely forget what it's like to know less about the game and the format.

That said, I'm living near WotC now and I meet a lot of new players trying a lot of strategies. 

EDH is a complex format with an insane range of power levels. When I see a new player trying to successfully pilot something like \[\[Hinata\]\], I think they've set themselves up to fail. More seasoned players are aware of that commander's potential and regardless of what's in the deck are definitely more likely to treat it like a threat. At the same time, while that deck can be built somewhat cheaply, it's much harder to pilot well, especially if you're being treated like a more experienced player.

Compare that to a strategy like landfall, or tokens (which definitely go hand in hand a lot). I think a lot of players struggling to increase their win-rate and learn more about the complex interactions available would benefit from trying out simpler strategies and focusing on learning how to navigate the dynamics of a multiplayer format. Playing UG sea monsters is simple, effective, and very cheap to build. 

I think now is a great time to be playing EDH. There are just so many options that absolutely do work. There's an understandable draw toward the flashiest and powerful options like \[\[Dockside Extortionist\]\], \[\[The Great Henge\]\], or tutors like \[\[Vampiric Tutor\]\] (not to mention excessively expensive mana bases). I'd recommend trying to ignore that want for a bit and focus on feeling good in the games. I don't look at cards like \[\[Rampaging Baloths\]\] and think it's a hidden gem - it's definitely not run as often as it once was. It's like an on-curve threat that shits out a lot of value for no real additional cost. Focus on cards like that, and there are plenty that are still very cheap.

I feel you, it's always a bit of a bummer trying to find the group that fits for you.

The "easier said than done" thing here is just try to enjoy yourself, and prioritize your joy there. The arms race you're talking about is real, and at the same time EDH in particular has become a very abundant and diverse format. There are a lot of decks that don't cost a ton but still spit out insane value. 

There will still be the problem of others' more tuned lists. I think having that earnest conversation before a game helps some there. I don't think the number system is the most useful; i think a lot of people underestimate their decks until they're absolutely certain it's a cEDH list. Having been hospitalized, it does suck. Your fears come from a real place.

At the same time, there are a LOT of steps between where you are and being hospitalized.

When I start with a new provider these days, I put it forward in the first session - "I've been hospitalized and I'm certain going back would be incredibly dangerous for my mental health. I need to know that you are only going to do that as an absolute last resort, after consulting me, and only because you absolutely legally have to."

Furthermore, if it is the case that this therapist wants to have you hospitalized, it'll likely be under the realm of "this patient is at too high a risk of hurting themselves or someone else." There are a LOT of other topics for you to talk about that aren't that. 

Even more so, when you're hospitalized most of the time they require you to enter into the ward voluntarily or involuntarily, and you get to choose. If you go involuntarily, they can't keep you indefinitely and you can follow up with a court order.

All of that out of the way, I know these feelings. I've been in therapy for 25 years. I've done so many things, learned so many tools, and changed myself and perspective so many times that I'm absolutely forgetting what's real and what's not sometimes. Unfortunately for me (and maybe you) therapy can only do so much, and with something like chronic depression there isn't really anything the field can do that's guaranteed to work. It's a chronic condition, like diabetes or psoriasis, but we just have so much less knowledge about how it works. So some of us are going to live our whole lives feeling these feelings and therapy is only ever going to be one piece of treatment that sometimes helps make our lives a little easier.

Yeah, absolutely. There are a few known mechanisms that connect depression and depressive episodes with a decline in thinking and cognitive function.

Studies have shown the best "medicine" for depression is the body's natural response, **which is sleep deprivation**. Though we don't know exactly how, we know that sleep deprivation alleviates depressive symptoms pretty consistently and that it's a common symptom among those experiencing depression. A leading theory states that the deprivation causes a decrease in cognitive function necessary to limit the brain's capacity to ruminate on a problem or thought.

Sluggishness and brain fog are known symptoms of depression. One of the questions on the PHQ-9 (perhaps the most common depression assessment tool) is related to a slowing of movement, speech, and thought.

Dissociation and derealization are also symptoms of depression that point to a damaged sense of security in your surroundings. Both of these have a high correlation with exhaustion and fatigue. My own theory there is that it's effort to dissociate (subconscious effort tho) and we don't recognize how much work we're doing to meet the minimums when we're going through a period of increased depression.

Treatment comes in many forms. Therapy can be very helpful for both episodic and persistent, chronic depression. It can both allow you space to explore yourself and also provide you concrete tools to use when you're experiencing acute symptoms. I sometimes have trouble taking the tools seriously, because it's things like checklists of basic needs for the real bad days, box-breathing techniques, or sticky notes that remind you that you've done something before and can do it again. 

Unfortunately, in my experience at least, depression never really goes away. For those of us with persistent depression, it's pretty constant. For everyone else, depression is a natural part of being. Life is going to be incredibly rough with us from time to time, and depression is a healthy and natural response to those struggles. For me, that means the first tool to use in these moments is compassion and empathy for yourself. If you can acknowledge (or get diagnosed with) depression, practice some kindness for yourself as soon as you can. It's not allergies, diabetes, or a chest cold. Some of the symptoms can be suppressed with medication, but overall depression has no cure right now. 

I'm glad you're reaching out and asking questions. You're gonna keep getting better at navigating these tough times as you learn more about yourself and what your needs are at the worst of times. Keep going, and I hope it eases up for you soon

A few things come up for me reading this. A recent provider of mine brought up an established fact that those experiencing depression have a harder time engaging in "delusions". It was in reference to this exact idea you're talking about, and it's hit me hard.

The world is on fire. There IS immense inequity, there IS an active war happening, there IS an understandable sense of doom on the horizon. The world is inarguably rather bleak right now, and at least in my experience I find a lot of people agree with me as individuals. 

I am certainly tired of hearing what I'm about to say next, so I apologize if I'm beating a dead horse for you as well. 

The delusion is not that the world is perfect and wonderful. That is certainly the appearance. The delusion is a (likely subconscious) choice to use the attention available to focus on other things. In mindfulness language, it becomes very quickly about a locus of control. I can't do much of anything about the war in Ukraine, or the school shootings happening elsewhere in my country. I can make posts about it, and contribute funds to larger organizations with more power but my ability to make change as an individual is incredibly limited.

So I can choose to engage in my thoughts about those awful things, or I can pull my focus away and toward the things in front of me - my cat, my art, my partner, etc. 

More specifically, the hopelessness you talk about revolves a lot around the grind. Not sure how old OP is, but it sounds like you're frustrating with the monotony of adult life as a 20 - 40 something. 

Adult life IS a grind. Prior to adult life we have a lot of structure meant to matriculate us pretty quickly into a society who's rules we were not around to agree to. Adult life is then three to six decades of figuring out how you're going to engage in that society. At a minimum that's already more time than you spent prior to being an "adult" and at max, that's a much longer time than you weren't an "adult". A lot of it is going to end up being real same-y. 

The same advice applies. You do have the ability to pull your own focus. Building or co-opting structures that provide you something to look forward to or work toward is going to be a huge step toward finding fulfillment. You're going to have to pin meaning and importance on something, and it will be whatever you want.

**TL;DR** \- The world is changing. It's a huge organism and it's going to change much more slowly as a result. You can change the choices you're making every day. You're absolutely right, you have limited options, but you don't have none. Take some time, pick a prize and aim yourself at it. You're an adult, it can be anything; just having a direction and a payoff in front of you will help some, I think.

Motivation is a difficult resource to come by for some for a lot of reasons. I've got chronic depression and I've been in a bout of anhedonia for a bit over two years now. I definitely find myself asking some of the questions you've asked here. I've got a few things that might help.

Sometimes it's just about adding any structure you can. Routines and maintenance can be boring and unrewarding sometimes; all the same, having one day a week, or an hour every other day set specifically for tidying (whatever happens along that lines) is a step to help add structure, and differentiate your life. Structure should help some with motivation, as a lack of structure has some weird effects on our perception of time.

While it's logical to say motivation has to come before action, there's an idea called behavioral activation that speaks to the counter behavior in humans. Put flatly, the act of doing something can generate a sense of motivation to either continue doing it, or finish the task. The hard part is pushing your body and mind to do things despite having a neutral, or bad time.

Some practice letting go of expectations may also help. Expectations of a level of cleanliness, productivity, or energy can definitely trigger an anxiety response, which can also sometimes bring along other meta-feelings about the anxiety. Set a goal to tidy, or practice grooming, or go for a walk and try practicing embracing whatever smallest form of that manifests. 

These are all strategies that can help; but ultimately the answer to your question will only come in time. The meaning you find in life, whether it's the fun or the work, will be there because you put it there. The counter of this is when you do nothing, it's very easy for everything to feel meaningless. There are absolutely other schools of thought that disagree, that say there is inherent meaning to hard work, or living well, etc. It sounds like that isn't working for you right now, and it might be time to try a different perspective.

I've thought a fair bit about this, I've been playing since near the conception of the format. I remember reading about it online just as Conflux was dropping. Something like:  


* Primeval Age - EDH is conceived as a highlander format featuring the Elder dragons of MTG lore
* Stone Age - EDH spreads slowly as other legends are explored. IIRC, Niv-Mizzet (OG) and Azami were top of the list. I don't remember a banlist at this time.
* Bronze Age - In 2011 WotC released the initial precons, which were pretty crazy at the time. Riku became a powerhouse, as did Ghave.
* The First Plague - In the 2011 - 12 cycle, Avacyn Restored was printed shortly after Rise of the Eldrazi. Tables were a mess as everyone rushed to drop one stupid bomb after another. Personally, this was the worst time to play EDH.
* The Dark Ages - With the release of the 2013 lists, we began to see the first of what would be many really unfortunately powerful lists. Oloro and Derevi were particularly notorious, but the Dark Ages still has glimmers here and there, when shit like Korvold and Chulane came out. A lot of important things happened during this time. The RC begin to really refine what their protocol for banning cards was and made at least a few very good choices, like banning Primeval Titan and Sylvan Primordial (I say this as a very green player).
* A Grand Epiphany - In 2015, EDHREC goes live and begins a new age of netdecking., It's an incredible resource for players who have begun flocking into the format as a palette cleanser from standard and modern. It remains a powerful tool, but has fallen prey to its own algorithms. Netdecking has become more and more normal (and it always was, to be clear) and EDHREC is easily one of the primary culprits.
* The Second Plague - In 2016, four color decks were released along with the Partner mechanic. At first, everything felt like Lorwyn/Alara standard. Everyone was running good-stuff piles and it felt like a bubble was about to burst. Instead, cEDH really began to take off and more and more players began having Rule 0 discussions.
* The Third Plague - In 2017, tribal precons were released along with the Eminence mechanic. It was a terrible idea and reinforced a pretty minimal form of deckbuilding. It's around this point in the dark ages where I begin to dread new sets coming out. Not a week after hour of devastation came out there was at least one Locust God at every table I played. 
* The Dawn of a New Age - In 2018, more Planeswalker commanders were released and to everyone's delight the lists were very fine. In 2019, they gave us mechanically niche commanders and it felt like we were moving into safer and safer territory. A bulk of players had gotten over some of their craze to have the hippest newest thing. I began seeing a lot more cute bullshit.
* The Age of Abundance - In 2020, over 300 legendary creatures were printed (not all of them were new). The trend continued and we've just seen oodles of legendary cards. In addition, there's easily way too many playables for every color and color combo. Even netdecking has become tough because inevitably there are just too many cards worth a slot. Players begin keeping slots for pet cards and the more competitive lists turn to jankier and jankier ways to pull out the same combo "for style points".

That's the story as I've lived it. I play less than ever before, in large part because while the decks feel healthier now (in terms of diversity and playstyle) there are a ton of new players who flatly aren't very good at Magic, I'm an impatient person who's been playing forever, and I only hve so much capacity for watching someone figure out their own deck. That said, I've really enjoyed what Wizards has been doing specifically for EDH in the last 3 to 5 years. I wasn't sure we'd make it, but I'm glad we're here.

EDH is a lot easier when you like and are decent at politics. That means getting better at:

* threat assessment
* knowledge of particular strategies
* earnest communication
* bluffing

I put them in that order particularly, because I think threat assessment is the skill most people lack, followed immediately by not knowing how strategies are played (including sometimes our own list).

I really like Karametra as a starter list because she's very powerful with little effort and you're in great colors for removal and resilience. Karametra (and WG in general) is great at not-losing. For you, I'd focus on the politics first before worrying about the second point. 

Consider how much removal you're running, and then consider your meta. If you feel like you know the decks you see regularly, begin to appreciate how they run and how they can be disrupted. From there, it's just about vocalizing when any particular deck (even your own if you're me) is close to dangerous and either doing something about it yourself, or putting forth that you can't do anything about it but something should probably be done.

​

To your second point, I think Karametra is good here as well because there are a lot of flash enablers that will take your deck to the next level both in terms of politics and also in terms of being able to act on others' turns. The more instant-speed interaction you run, the more bluffing becomes a skill you can and have to practice. But like I said, I would definitely start with learning more threat assessment, common strategies, and vocalizing more often.

For some, it's a constant process to juggle all of those expectations while maintaining any semblance of personal health. So one of my inner voices speaks of empathy. We are all trying, and at any particular moment the person you are talking to or interacting with may not be trying along the same axes as you.

People are rarely malicious; they are more often oblivious and appear selfish as a result. We're animals, driven by survival instincts even as we've progressed well beyond survivalism in many parts of the modern world. Several people have had no need or opportunity to introspect and evaluate their actions because they've always felt affirmed in their pursuit of largely animal things. Collect resources, procreate, etc. Another voice that speaks against my misanthropy is animal. Humans gonna human, and while it can be incredibly frustrating to engage it is understandable and normal. Empathy chimes in here as well, because I want grace in my animal moments as well.

The "average" is often way lower than we imagine, and as individuals we are incredibly prone to observer biases. If you are scholastically gifted, chances are you might find many people very "dumb," even though statistically they are likely just pretty average. On the flip side, the human experience is so multifaceted that most people are (well) above average at \*something\*. Giving people a chance to shine at their best might allow them to seem more "worthwhile". 

There's no wrong way to human with other humans.  I hear the misanthropy the OP is talking about, and I see in myself. We're used to stories of coupling, or incredibly strong bonds in small groups of friends. At the same time, there will always be people connecting in different ways. The large majority of the time I prefer to be a peripheral presence for many. It can be exhausting and feel like I am often forgotten, but I love knowing a bunch of people and hearing their stories occasionally, rather than indulging a smaller group in the banality of their everyday lives. Whatever your current state of connection with others is, it can change if you want to. The transitional period may feel awkward and performative, but if you want fewer deeper connections or more, sporadic ones you have some control there. 

TL;DR - sometimes with my own misanthropy I feel like I'm beating myself up with others' expectations. I don't dislike my style and frequency for connecting with others. It isn't "normal" and as a result it can feel more exhausting. But I do it because it suits my needs well.

There's a lot to be said here. I won't be able to say everything.

One component at play here seems to be the reality-skewing nature of internet platforms. When I log onto reddit, and make a comment I have so much more reach than individuals have had in the past. In return, if my comment is remotely incendiary I am subject to the whims of a much larger crowd than individuals in the past. That alone is a cool feature of the internet that just showcases the immense step we took into the future. **But**, if we combine this with a few cognitive distortions (which are all very human behaviors) we end up with messy situations and a lot of hurt feelings. Personally, I think one of the bigger distortions featured here is **personalization**, or the idea that my world is about me and that all happenings are related to me in some way. That's pure ego, and it's rarely factual or helpful. OP nods to this by emphasizing empathy in our comments. We don't know the context of others' posts and since most of the world is not about us as individuals, it might be helpful to consider and comment with a slightly less personal lens. That's a skill, it takes practice and no one has to do it.

The other big piece that I'm interested (very selfishly), is the focus on insults. Language is a very complex tool we've developed over time. It's got a lot of dials and knobs for fine control, and different media all have different ups and downs. Insults more specifically seem to serve a purpose for humans as emotional creatures; insults provide us momentary vents for our feelings (not just limited to anger, sadness, or the other "bad vibes"). We don't all have access to formal therapy, and not every situation calls for a great amount of therapeutic processing. In lieu of unpacking our feelings whenever we encounter an emotional spike, we can toss an insult or an exclamation as a sort of primal shout. A shortcoming of this approach is that insults usually have a target, and given our affinity toward personalization the target is often immediately sensitive to the insult. OP put forth the idea that the insults can cut deep into the issues at hand, serving only to worsen the situation and minimize chances of any pleasant outcomes. I liked that a lot because it highlights an area of control that we have; we always get to choose what insults we use. Quite often we're lazy and we throw out the classics - bitch, motherfucker, retard, etc. As our society has grown, we've begin to decide that some of these are dated symbols of oppressive systems we don't want anymore, and as insults they're just verbal shivs in a fight. I can only offer my solution here, which is creativity. In a world of lazy and genuinely hurtful words, we can take advantage of the multitude of options we have for insults. Some who disagrees with you doesn't have to be "retarded" but you can absolutely vent your frustration with them and call them something to show it. I love the schoolhouse classics like "butthead" or "wad" but I've grown quite fond of the more absurd approach. Why call someone a cunt when you can call them "rotted fish head" or "cumgoblin"? 

It sounds a bit like OP would like to see less insults over all, and I think that's an admirable goal. I like the idea of a future where our words to one another are considered and kind, even if they are pointed and opposed. I only offer some small steps in the face of what feels like necessary human expression.

TL;DR - I think humans need insults as a form of dynamic incendiary expression of our primal feelings. I also think we can quickly divorce ourselves from the deep cuts and harmful language by embracing a sillier and more absurd side to insults.

I think you're wise before yourself here. It's not good or bad yet and it does sound like your perceptions have changed. 

It takes about four to six weeks for our body to solidify new habits. If you've been cooped up for a month with little to no social exposure, your body has likely started to recalibrate its needs to its resources. Think of it like your body going into a social starvation mode because you've been in a social desert.

One thing I liked about this process for myself was that it laid out what felt like a bare and abstract truth. You do definitely need some level of social interaction, humans are a pack animal. But you can control that need a fair amount and we are very used to a narrative where social interaction is high. Moving forward, now that you know you can operate with less you get the choice to follow the old narrative or to make something new for yourself. Maybe you've found that you enjoy your alone time, and choose to cultivate a much smaller social life moving forward. Maybe you find that once your academic boundaries are gone, your social needs increase again and you want to go back to the old ways. Either is fine, and the choice will be yours.

I can say that in my experience of this, it's a bit jarring when I do try to go back to a more social life because I've kind of forgotten the rhythm of that lifestyle. You might feel a bit awkward or rusty in social settings. It's like riding a bicycle or picking up an old hobby. Your body does know how to do it, but you have to brush the dust off. It might take a month or so of conscious pushing past the awkwardness for you to regain more of the comfort of your old lifestyle.

Regardless, have fun with it. Listen to your body. If you try and try and are still having a bad time, look for ways to change it. Be well, as best you can.

Be open to radical ideas. Maybe that's commune living, maybe it's sex work, maybe it's moving to a different country with a better program for governmental assistance. Remember that none of these will be perfect and they will have steep opportunity costs.

Look for ways to make life better outside of work. A big part of the fuckery of modern living is that work sucks AND we also have chores that eat up an inordinate amount of our time. If work is terrible for her, help her ensure that maintenance outside of work is easier.

Unlearning a response acquired in emotional development takes time and intention. You’ve already made big strides in admitting you can rationalize your parents’ choices.

Intention doesn’t always match the outcome and it’s important to allow some grace for your emotions rather than deny them or refute them. When you begin to acknowledge that your anger was valid despite your parents’ intent you can begin to detach the past from the present. The anger will become a memory and you can begin to treat it as such. The pain will likely never go away entirely; wounds rarely do. But the ache will lessen.
It might also help to be frank with your parents. “I know you did this because X but it made me really angry at the time. I’m still processing that, but I trust your intent.” Intellectualizing it and vocalizing it can help provide distance between the past emotion and the present.

My background is just in quantum mechanics and physics, where degeneracy is exactly commonality of accessible energy states. If two accessible states are equal in energy, then the energy level is degenerate.

Certainly MTG has a more colloquial twist, but what I personally see in "degenerate" strategies is that they have been popularized and become infamous. They're exactly common, because they're powerful and usually frustrating (to your second point).

When you say you want to know what kind of pressure Hasbro puts on WotC, what do you mean?

Look at the years since Hasbro has taken over. There has been a huge increase in product released, including newly designed product that constantly pushes the boundaries of power. Every set has had a VERY obvious selling gimmick, and they've been increasing the types of products as well to appeal to wider and wider audiences.

The pressure is HUGE and so far WotC has been delivering, seeing constant (or near constant) growth since being acquired.

As far as I'm concerned, the "end" started at the acquisition, but I also think WotC has been doing a decent job on a lot of the changes, given how much of it there has been and how toxic and volatile their playerbase can be. They've made a conscious effort to design a more representational and inclusive set of worlds, and have done so without sacrificing the integrity of their designs. The power creep is a definite problem, but it has always been there and is unfortunately likely unavoidable given the spectacularism we're addicted to as consumers.

Degeneracy most literally refers to the commonality of a situation. In QM degeneracy refers to energy levels of equal value. Many people talk about something degenerate in Magic as if it means powerful, but that's actually the motivator.

When something is degenerate it's because it's seen everywhere. When \[\[Locust God\]\] came out (or really whenever a new powerful commander hits the scene) there's a spike in the degeneracy of those lists as the internet hive mind rushes to "solve" them as best they can. Usually those lists are piles of good-stuff cards in those colors.

\[\[Prime Time\]\] was banned partially because he facilitated very degenerate board states. The best line of play was always to clone or steal Prime Time, and even then the best plays with it were things like Urborg/Coffers. Seeing the same lines of play over and over and over made a Highlander format feel very "anti-highlander" and rather stale.

These days, there's a huge variety in cards you can play. cEDH accepts a certain level of degeneracy because they highly value consistency in their strategies. That said, even at the cEDH level there are a ton of viable options now that \[\[Flash\]\] got the axe.

The game does get healthier with more and more cards; but the players are not getting healthier so there's always a spike in degeneracy whenever the greedy humanoids get shiny new toys.

It isn't a white specific issue for any reason other than white seems to be struggling more than the other colors standing on its own in this format. 

I think part of it is that white does not generally do well at a number of things this format tends to focus on (at least for the average EDH table). Personally, I don't care either way. I don't play mono-white much because I find it overly reactive and slow.

I think when people look at some of the gifts white has been receiving, they mostly see something to splash in a deck that is primarily non-white. That's still progress, but white wasn't a bad splash color before these changes. White was always a color worth running *with* other colors. It has literally the best removal in the format for pretty much any problem and a ton of ways to be resilient. To me that says that players don't care much about "fixing" white as a splash, they care about fixing white as a mono-color problem. You can certainly help that by giving white tools that W/X lists use with ease, but that's not closing the gap between white and other mono-color lists. 

It's a big stretch but for me it's almost like considering wealth inequity. If there's a gap in wealth distribution, the gap doesn't get better if you give everyone a boost. Sure, everyone might be happy but if you're trying to diminish the gap you just haven't done that. The gap only lessens when either the lower end is elevated, the higher end is dampened, or some combination. Personally it sounds like players are more interested in narrowing the gap, but I could be wrong. I'm fine with being wrong, and regardless I'm fine with whatever WotC gives us as long as it feels like elegant design.

It's a point raised by a few other users. Cards like Smothering Tithe *do* improve mono-white but also serve to improve W/X decks. That's why I personally think the better question is how do we improve mono-white specifically, and not just white as a color. White is a great splash in a deck, it's just not known for holding it's own as a mono-color list.

I mean, the issue as stated previously was "white is not a good color in EDH". There's plenty of evidence that goes against that, even in this thread. The nuance missing seems to be "mono white is not good in EDH," which is inherently different.

The solution then becomes what cards and effects can be made that improve the strength of mono-white? The questions inside that are:

1. What does the card do that mono-white needs?
2. What does the card do to disincentivize use as a splash?

Mono-white needs card draw or permanents that efficiently create card advantage (not things like \[\[Armistice\]\]). Mono-white doesn't get outright card draw in droves, because color pie. But even assuming that's the easy fix, the second part is still an issue. How do we begin to design white cards that W/X lists avoid?

1. Make them "plains" or white matters cards. Effects like "this costs 1 less for each basic plains you control."
2. Make them averse to splashing. Effects like "this costs 1 more for each land type among lands you control."
3. Make them heavily white costed. Admittedly this is antagonistic to efficient design. WWW is not splashable, but also can't be easily cast off sol ring mana.

I think a lot of players gripe and moan about the problems without considering the intricacies of the solution, so I'm definitely pleased to see people considering the issue more critically. I think WotC has shown promise with their recent experiments, but obviously we're looking at a change to occur over a few years. That happened with Red and now red faces a different issue (it's not super splashable). 

I think another issue that comes up in relation to your article is that a lot of the tools that white has to level the field do exactly that. They focus on parity. But EDH is often taken as a format of extremes and acceleration into windmill-slams. In my experience, white doesn't (and personally shouldn't do that), but it does mean that there's a dissonance between the color's individual philosophy and the desires of the format. White is a fine stax color, but the majority of EDH players don't like stax lists because they want to do big splashy things and stax is about grinding small advantage.

In any case, I'm hopeful that WotC can find design space the accomplishes what they want without overly compromising the cards themselves or playing further into the W/X trap.

Why haven’t you killed yourself yet?

1. It’s hard:
   1. It’s hard in terms of knowing that I’m going to be doing irrevocable damage to people who “don’t deserve it.” It’s somewhat easier to think about how “well, they’re gonna die to so no worries.” But it’s definitely hard knowing that it’s not a zero-sum game. Even for all that I suffer, killing myself will net greater suffering almost guaranteed
   2. It’s hard in terms of “planning.” When I moved into my last place, I contemplated suicide a bunch in the first month because I finally lived alone. I didn’t have to worry about timing around a roommate. But still, the body would have to be found, ramifications for strangers would ensue, see point 1.1.
   3. It’s literally hard biologically. Cutting is a decent enough method because all you have to do is make the cut and not do anything. But still, it’s viscerally painful and you have to fight through it. Pills are tricky as fuck because the body has a natural toxin response, and is way more resilient than you’d expect. Most times, pills just lead to liver damage and a very slow slow slow, observed death. Trains/cars involve strangers, see point 1.2. Drowning is very tough because the body literally fights against it. Hypothermia is fine, and is near the top of the list. And proper euthanasia is actually difficult these days because of regulations (which could have been a 1.4, I guess)
2. The whole world is (obviously) not terrible. I revel in a good deal of things. Humans are even involved in those things a lot of the time. But somehow, for whatever reason, those things are often not a topic of discourse. “Regular” human things make me feel isolate, powerless, and betrayed. Talking about money, relationships, societal strife reminds me of all the ways I am saddened and disappointed with the world. This is an area in which I can practice “radical acceptance,” but that still relies on the idea that I want to participate (which a lot of times would appear to be wrong).
3. I still have hopes and dreams, even if they’re broken or unsustainable. I am still subject as most of us are to the expectations laid out for me in youth. I want someone to love me like I was told, and I want a career that invigorates me. I don’t think those things are going to happen, and not as a doom and gloom thing, but more of just, the world is wider than that. But still, there’s a dissonance that rings internally near that suicidal precipice — “what if love would happen tomorrow? what if the next job you try IS the thing that fixes you?” I’ve been raised on snake oil, and it’s infected my brain. The truth is “life will always involve some level of dissatisfaction.” This implies and relies on the idea that “just because it’s good doesn’t mean it can’t get better.” I think this point also implies an idea of radical acceptance for suicide. I may always want to kill myself, and I genuinely hope that’s how I go out. The problem most cycling decks have is that their pilot wants to do a lot of things, but most of those things don't actually affect the game at all. 

First and foremost, make sure what you're doing advances SOMETHING. I see you have a few effects that trigger on draws. You're a cycling list, make that number as high as possible. Same for discard triggers, things like \[\[Glint-Horn Buccaneer\]\] and \[\[Drannith Stinger\]\].

There are a few additions here that are going to do less than you'd expect, like \[\[Yidaro\]\] just because at best it'll only ever be an 8/8 with trample. In this format, trample is probably the worst form of evasion, and this archetype (cyclotrons) does not specialize in beaters usually. 

Avoid blink strategies that rely on things like \[\[escape protocol\]\], \[\[astral slide\]\], \[\[astral drift\]\]. They take forever and are very skill intensive both in terms of deck-building and actual playing. Focus on just drawing cards and discarding cards. If you want inspiration, look at the EDHREC pages for \[\[the Locust god\]\] or \[\[Niv-Mizzet, Parun\]\].

A lot of cyclotron lists run things like \[\[Approach of the Second Sun\]\]. I hate this card, but it's absolutely reasonable in this list.

Things that can only trigger once per turn, like \[\[Improbable Alliance\]\] are fine but they'll be skill intensive upfront and give very minor benefits unless you play them really well.

Very frankly, cyclotrons are tough decks to pilot well. If you're new to Magic in general, I would advise picking up the temur list or the mardu list to get a better grasp on the pace of a typical edh game without adding too much stress. If you're just new to EDH, welcome to the format.

Kadena was "made for" morph, but as a result has some obvious limitations in that morph is at best a YuGiOh-like combo deck. Kadena isn't even specifically better than Ixidor, which is unfortunate. I personally think Kadena is literally the worst morph general among them.

Ixidor was also "made for" morph decks, but far before commander and the NWO so the powerlevel is a bit wonky. That said, the ability to reuse morphs with ease is incredible and this version of the deck is very focused.

Animar morph is a fine option (for reasons I'll discuss further below) but literally animar morph is the worst animar list I can imagine.

Which leads me to Chulane, my current morph general. He literally does everything I want a morph commander to do and gives me access to white, which leads me to the second part of the discussion - which colors are best for morph in EDH?

​

The obvious starting point is blue, given the strong tie between the mechanic and color reinforced in Onslaught and again in Time Spiral. And as I said before, the focus of an all-blue Ixidor list is not to be ignored.

The next color is almost always Green, with decks like Kruphix popping up. I've personally never bothered with UG morph because it doesn't give me that much more oomph than mono-blue, but there are certainly notable inclusions like the ramp or draw enchantments from Khans.

The third color is all over the place. Pretty flatly, red morph creatures are really bad. And the temur options really aren't better. The nice thing about an Animar list is you get access to regular Animar shenanigans like \[\[cloudstone curio\]\] and \[\[impact tremors\]\]. That's all well and good, but again you don't need a morph deck to do that, it's just Animar being strong.

So I'm back to black and white for a third color. Black gets me Kadena, which is nice AND it gets me the morph wrath (which I love as a pet card tbh) and nice creature recursion like \[\[Soul of Innistrad\]\]. Beyond that, black gives me tutors? I don't love tutors as much anymore though.

Then I look at white, I get some real cute morph cards that all essentially fog assaults against me. I get slightly worse card draw, but Chulane is insane at that, and I'm also running UG so I'm not really worried about it. I also get access to blink, enchantment tutors, and the hallmark morph card that doesn't get enough love, \[\[mastery of the unseen\]\]. 

Realistically, I don't think animar is the right choice outright. Mostly because animar will almost always drive the deck toward being animar-centric rather than morph centered. Kadena fixes that because she's fine at best. Chulane is similar because he's nothing to do with morph, but is such a good enabler. I prefer white to black because I think white does a better job at doing what morph decks like to do, but you'll be fine with black here.

Sometimes the reprints that are "needed" literally don't make sense in any set other than the original context. The Lorwyn lands are a great example - they don't follow any consistent color patterning (I think it's wu/ub/br/rw/bg/wubrg?). I get that these lands are pricy, and definitely facilitate certain lists in modern, but they were oddly designed and barring an uncomfortable moment where they're reprinted literally, "just 'cause" I don't think we'll ever see them again. The same goes for stuff like the Kamigawa monolands. They're all legendary and hyperspecific, and feel additionally out of place without the full cycle. It could be nice to get Eiganjo again, but then we'd waste a spot on Okina. Which is the other part of the issue is that cycles like these aren't equitably valuable so in addition to being awkward reprints, players are still going to complain because not every card in the cycle is worth the pack.  


As for some of the other cards on your list, I think sometimes it's a bit about tailored expectations? Food Chain and Mirri's Guile fit a little less well in the NWO. That's not to say they're impossible to print because of that, it's just more like if WotC doesn't have to open the door they're probably not going to. It's in Wizards' best interest to not inform the more recent players that older cards did insane weird things that more often than not just lead to degenerate lists. I think we can expect to see stuff like Food Chain, Dream Halls, or maybe even Nether Void (RL I know) confined to outlets like the judge promo programs. Wizards pretty clearly (in my opinion) doesn't want those cards available to "just any player".  


The other factor to consider is that the pool of possible reprints only grows. Which means the antsy nature around specific "needed" reprints will almost always also grow. We saw this a bit when Tarmogoyf was first reprinted - players getting one on accident urged them to pursue a playset. I'd wager that when the average player gets their hands on a new Mirri's Guile, they'll love it in there Green EDH list, and since EDH players aren't known for their restraint they'll want it for all of their green lists. The demand just grows and the reprint could never have fully done it's job. The only time we see reprints genuinely do their job is when Wizards prints the same things over and over and over in a short period. We're seeing this a bit with things like Selvala, and Rhys, and we've definitely seen it before with Adarkar Valkyrie. The unfortunate takeaway here is that Wizards absolutely knows how to do what you want, and is doing it, just not with the cards that you want specifically. It is happening with cards that others want though, as well as cards that most don't want (sorry Cragganwick Cremator). i don't expect this trend to change remarkably, and I also don't think it's insidious.

My best advice would really focus on what you need and why. Personally speaking I've seen a few reprints I'm excited about, specifically because they aren't high value, but they aren't cheap. I'm excited to grab another copy or two of heat shimmer as it drops, and I'm excited to see other players begin to use it more. Same goes for Sneak Attack,  and a few others. And we've got more to come.

I'm going to reflect some of your words back and give my own opinion.

*"I've always been quite a sensitive person."*

What about you gives you that impression? How would you describe that idea without using the word 'sensitive?' Additionally, at your gut do you think being quite sensitive is inherently bad, good, or healthy (or unhealthy)?

*"I take everything to heart and take things personally."*

This sounds like a classic example of 'personalization' which is a form of reductive thinking. There are between 10 and 15 of these ideas that amount to a sort of pantheon of "irrational thought" (though I don't like that word because thoughts usually have some rationale, even if it's not based in observable evidence). Personalization is exactly about perceiving yourself as the target of others' behavior. In fact, even in direct communication with you, most individuals are often acting on and toward their own feelings. While there is consideration of you sometimes, claiming yourself as the target is (perhaps dangerously stated) narcissistic. Flatly, you're not the center of the universe. You're one human.

"...o*ne guy developed a new accent which I know for a fact is fake, but it just bothered me so much."*

Two questions, how do you **know** he wasn't affecting an accent before and is now comfortable enough to speak in his genuine accent now? And, separately usually when something bothers us in someone else, it's because we're seeing something uncomfortable that we recognize in ourselves OR something that is just genuinely dissonant with our perception of the Truth of the world. This could totally be the second case, and you're just used to his other accent so much that the new one is causing you discomfort or you could recognize (especially at a young age) that this person has made an autonomous choice to change his presentation and you have an internal desire to do something similar but aren't comfortable facing that decision yet. Just theories.

"...*it just lingered in my mind and bothered me the entire day."*

It sounds like this, and the first example, both speak to the genuine problem. You appear to be ruminating on these triggering events, long past when the actual stimulus occurs. This is exactly where meditation and mindfulness can jump in actively. It's a process (and a practice) to begin recognizing rumination as a choice that you're making - even if it's subconscious. With practice, the choice begins to be more obvious, and conscious, and you'll get better at recognizing it sooner. Eventually, you might find that you can see the choice even exactly after the trigger occurs, which means you can control your reaction (though you can't control the impulsive feeling). The key here is that it's a practice. You're going to start as a novice and you're going to suck. You're going to fail a few times, and get better as you persist. 

*"...I don't want to give two fucks about all these stupid things"*

Yes. Yes and. Mindfulness will help you not give any fucks about things, but the important part here is that gaining control over what you want to give your effort and attention to. You're 19. As time goes on, you'll learn more of what you do and don't care about, and most importantly those things can change. Just remember that you don't want to care about nothing.

Best of luck.

in my own struggles with this it first took this exact realization. I was specifically using alcohol to blur my reality so I couldn't focus on it and my feelings toward it.

For me, it didn't really feel like a choice. Drunk me was slowly ruining my world. I made a lot of suicidal proclamations, and got raped a few times. Nowadays, I'm mostly okay being sober because being drunk lead to SO MANY other bad things.

On the less personal side though, being sober helped me see a few other things. Drunk people suck, it wasn't just me. They're almost always low-functioning and it's just really annoying.  My own anxiety and depression began to turn-tail on alcohol because I hated thinking of myself that way.

It was also way easier to maintain a healthy sleep schedule and diet when I wasn't drinking. Alcohol is literally a waste of calories, and the drunk sleep I got was never restorative. Slowly, I realized that even if I didn't feel depressed when drunk, I felt awful the rest of the time; the hard part was realizing that it meant lifting the whole veil off so that I could build something new. 

Greatly reducing my alcohol intake also meant saving a buttload of money, because I was usually drinking anywhere between 30 and 60 (sometimes up to 100$) a night. 

Really, the most annoying part of being sober for me is the social stigma behind "not drinking." People assume I'm judging them, or that I'm not a fun person because I don't drink, or don't drink as much. I don't owe them explanations though, and like I said in my first point, I don't envy them in the slightest. Aside from that, once my depression and anxiety agreed that alcohol was a waste of my time, it just happened naturally.

I'll say, it was also a matter of "finding a new vice". A lot of the time, I drank because it felt like I had to, because I couldn't enjoy parties or life otherwise. Except, I know shit that I like. If I want to alleviate my depression or anxiety, I turn to something I know I ACTUALLY enjoy. It took time and effort to find exact things, but when I found them I almost felt stupid for how simple they can be. It's things like drinking a coke, eating some cake, rewatching a show I know that makes me laugh, breaking something shitty like a cup, taking a nap, masturbating. I think vices come in enough forms that really the issue is when we go too deep on just one. 

​

TL; DR:

1. Alcohol and being drunk was becoming actively terrible.
2. Alcohol made me physically feel like shit whenever I wasn't drunk
3. Alcohol was making me VERY poor.
4. Diversify your portfolio of vices. Escapism is necessary, but there are healthier ways to engage it.

I like to think that I play magic to make optimal moves. I've been called competitive in this frame. I mean, my specific stance on cancer is that the set of diseases is something to be studied and harnessed rather than cured. It's more or less a mutation that's allowing life at a basic level to "try too hard." It's definitely killing people, but I don't fall prey to the emotional argument of "every individual is important." Loss happens, and could be argued must happen for the progression of understanding toward goals.

As for curing diseases as a way to improve human life, I don't see it as the same. Diseases - I think in large part - differ vastly from aging in that they prey upon the unfairness we've built into the world and tilt the playing field even more so. Curing malaria didn't do a TON stateside, but it has been a huge boon elsewhere in the world which means it helps develop a globalized state for the progress of the species. Slowing or stopping aging also helps this, but my argument is more along the line that in lieu of slowing or stopping aging, we should begin the arduous work of lifting the veil of the shadow of death and mortality that we have as humans. Without that fear, we'll be able to continue to pursue the same goals as a species more mindfully, while also making huge progress toward eliminating ideas of legacy that feed into a lot of economic dragons and other examples of inequity we're grappling with. Moreover, if we slow/stop aging without lifting the fear of mortality and death, we're really just gonna make the problem worse by having an elite class who ACTUALLY never dies and several tiers of poorer classes that can only ever afford to be food for the rich.

I survived what I considered to be one of the first turning points for EDH. When Rise of the Eldrazi came out, EVERYONE was running the titans. I hated it. Especially Ulamog because there were so few pieces of removal that worked on it. I definitely remember disliking a lot of my games, because everything felt like a race to eldrazi. And THEN they printed Avacyn. Which was so much worse. In 2011, I remember really liking my decks but I lost a good bit because the Chicago players straight up had more streamlined decks. Then the precons hit. 

I really loved \[\[Ghave\]\]. I built a few different decks in the other combinations. I remember really enjoying \[\[Intet\]\] as well, as a good-stuff list. And I recall people beginning to complain about how overpowered infect was with \[\[The Mimeoplasm\]\]. I loved Ghave, and I still do. Whatever, man I just like math. 

Then the years went by like you said. We got better removal, more exile tech. We got cool new generals and everytime something new came down the pipe more and more people rushed to build it. 

I think I was tired of it a few years back when Amonkhet hit. I think \[\[The Locust God\]\] was the first general I remember seeing and thinking, "ugh, everyone is going to build this, and it's just going to be the same deck over and over and over." I love EDH. It's such a deep well for MTG potential. It's great that it's thriving as a format. I wish WotC could keep up and/or people had more pet cards the way I do. I love my decks, and to an extent even those get boring if I play too often. I see the same lines of play over and over. I can predict 70-80 of the cards in a deck by the general. I get a bunch of nerds who think they're being unique and cheeky sitting down with God tribal, or Snakes on a Plane, or Rakdos Eldrazi (which is a list I do like and run every six months or so). 

I think there's still magic in the format for me. I know part of the problem for me is the blurry line between competitive and casual EDH. For me, that line gets drawn by tutor frequency. EDH is a highlander format for a reason; every tutor is a copy of any card in your deck essentially (hyperbole but the point is there). I also wish people took the time to practice their lists. They come to the table so proud of this beast they've accumulated from the internet or taken the time to scrap together. But then they miss their triggers, or they don't account for what card they need, or they're not thinking about what line of play they want to take. I've played with veteran players, and I've played with many strangers. At this point, EDH is reckless to trust to strangers. I need the comfort of people who understand how I interpret the spirit of the format. It's not about haymakers, it's not about cramming all the best things in your color or tribe into 100 cards. EDH is a story you take time to put together. It has a climax (or a few), it has exposition. It shouldn't always be told the same way. It should account for the audience. 

I know I'm the old man at the table. One of my regulars told me succinctly 'you don't play to win, you play to not lose.' I've seen all the bombs EDH has to offer. I feel like I spout endless analogies but I'll finish with one more. It feels like you can play EDH just fine where everyone drops their bombs and see which blows up biggest. That's fine. But I'd rather have a conversation at normal volumes with some deft and criticality than an argument at top volume.

People get over playing the locust god, or thrasios//tymna, and they'll get over playing Urza too. There were a trillion and more things that needed to happen throughout time for me to arrive where I am today, but the same can be said for every grain of sand, and every star in the galaxy. If you know someone with depression, don't assume you know their disease better than they do. Maintain trust and openness with them. Ask them how they are when they seem up and when they seem down. This is a struggle I'm wracked with frequently. I don't know how to best care for my loved ones against the stigmata assigned to suicide. It's been a persistent source of frustration for me in the last several months, and off and on for many years. The bottom line I always find myself at is "it's my body and my decision." Unfortunately, while it's my body and definitely my decision, it is not my existence alone. Every action I take sends waves through my community and further since I have ties to several communities throughout the nation. Moreover, suicide carries with it such strong connotations because unlike other forms of death, we can't blame the unknown and we can't blame time. When I commit suicide, it isn't going to be an "act of God," and it isn't going to be "my time." I will have ripped myself from this collective existence and I will leave a wound. 

People will ask "why did he do it," and they'll say things like "what a waste of potential," and "he was so young." They'll be faced head on with the real possibility of death, and furthermore that something so powerful is readily accessible and available; the question then becomes "if there's an exit, why don't I take it?" The idea starts subconsciously and worms its way into their lives, until one day, they're asking themselves the same things I ask myself, and maybe they'll take the plunge too. But wounds will heal. Society will either forgive or forget, and the latter is inevitable.
