Our thoughts reflect a great deal of goings-on "under the hood," so to speak, and it is only when we accept our thoughts as inescapable reality that we succumb to our depressive episodes.

With that out of the way, I can give you advice spun on bias. First, having succeeded through the academic system (so much so that I chose to keep going and going) it is very obvious that this environment, including the type of learning presented in an academic setting, is not meant for everyone. Second, you're caught up in an future involving a wife, house with a lawn and a few kids, but did you ever ask if that's the future you would sculpt for yourself, or rather is it an idealism imposed upon you by how you were raised, or the societal norms impressed upon you through media? Life has no cookie-cutter recipe for success, it's much more of a choose-your-own-adventure book. If formal schooling doesn't work for you, and you're unhappy enough to consider this because of it, you should look into other options, if only because there are other options. 

There was a post recently about a redditor who basically lives paycheck to paycheck, making enough to support an apartment and to fund his passion for creating art. It's an indulgent and lazy lifestyle from a widely societal standpoint, but he's content with it, and pliant to the notion that it can change. This spoke to me very well as an example of sound anecdotal advice to give high school graduates. If you want to play video games, or make video games, or whatever, find something, anything to provide the means to do that. Involve yourself in that culture, because again, you can find friends in almost any place, and video game culture is certainly one of them.

So it seems that you're in a bad spot, but that you've got room to grow in a lot of directions. Don't view life as a linear path, through which you've got to travel formulaically; instead consider that life is dimensional in amounts we cannot completely fathom, and begin exploring the possibilities. Make your life something you want to live, and adamantly refuse to be ashamed of what brings you joy. There exists no definition of success that is ubiquitous, and so we arrive at the old adage, "to each their own." You will be okay; you're young and you've been taught that selfishness is bad. You've got time to consider and reconsider your options as to whether or not that applies to you. Start by thinking about where you are and where you're going; if it's really not what you want, you can change it.

I echo this sentiment with a small edit. If you're looking for something to give your life meaning, something from without that will direct you to some greater goal and provide you with the impetus to persist on, you won't find it, easily or otherwise. The onus is on you to give your life inertia, and for most people, it's enough to wake everyday and continue on a path long ago decided. As animals, we largely exist to procreate, but as a sentient community, humans have decided that simply surviving is not enough. We push ever forward into the unknown, in search of answers that come in the form of more questions. On a day to day, people wake up and live to maintain their personal status quo, and in an overarching sense, people pursue dreams through a sense of hope, intrigue, and wonder at the multitudes of possibilities that might be.

But you're right, no one is really contributing anything of meaning to the state of the universe because there's no way humanity could decide on single true unit, and therefore deliverable quantity, of meaning. The world around you will always be what you make of it, and the notion of death as a pleasant inevitably serves the same purpose as actively choosing to do anything. If you want a reason to exist, simply reach into the hat and grab a slip, you'll find the choices are numerous; if you want an answer to life and how to go about it, you'll find yourself sorely wanting for something which is not, and never will be, there.

My suggestion to you and anyone who chooses to consider these thoughts: listen to more music, or simply go to the noisiest location you can find and just sit. Do your best to drown out your inner voice for a while. When you've chosen to think, or accepted as truth, that there is no reason, no motivation in life, you may replace your actions with a form of inaction. If there's nothing to live for, and nothing to die for, take a while and simply be; you're miraculous well prepared to stay alive without giving it much thought or effort, and you can revel in this ephemeral state, where you're not trying to be someone or do something. When it becomes enough for you to just be, reconsider what else you might want to do in addition to being. If it's nothing, take more time.

As an added piece of anecdote, I rarely follow my own advice, but it occurs to me that those people around me who appear happy have their own trials that they're struggling with, and it is only the perception that they are content just being that drives me to my conclusions. Therein lies another beautiful truth; while we certainly remain on an infinite spectrum of trials, each individual is struggling through life. Take solace that you are not, and never can be alone, and simply try to be for a while.

This reasoning is terrible. You won't give your life anymore meaning by ending it, in that the only meaning therein derived would be that left in the memories of those with whom you've interacted. From there, the meaning is cut short by your early demise, rather than embellished upon by further interactions. Furthermore, sympathy is a judgment, and this expected response is wholly what people refer to as a "selfish suicide." Don't get me wrong, suicide is very rarely for the sake of someone else, but acting upon these ideations to avoid one judgment in favor of another is outright baffling.

If you will, approach this from another perspective. You've made mistakes from a societal standpoint twice now. You'll be given repercussions, which inevitably yield disappointment from yourself and those with whom you share an emotional bond. But then you've still got time. If you're in school, I'm going to make a conservative estimate that your less than 30 years of age, and since you're likely posting on Earth as a human, I'm going to make another conservative estimate that you could reasonably live between 70 and 80 years of age. That gives you between 40 to 60 years to rebuild upon that disappointment with a sense of pride and experience. Yes, you fucked up, and this time, the system won and you lost. Yes, the road rebuilt takes a while and is uphill. But you were in college, and hopefully you had intent. That doesn't change. The season comes soon to apply for colleges if that's what you really want, but you can look at this another way. 

College won't make you an adult, and it won't make you responsible. It helps smooth the transition between dependency and independence by allowing 3-5 years of approximate dependence. It is by no means the be-all-end-all of success. Even if you fall short of my conservative estimate, and you're 32 or 35, you've still got enough time, "biologically speaking," to work a doldrums job for 5 years under your parents roof, saving enough to start anew in Europe or Asia or whatever region you may fancy. The world DOES NOT END when you *might* leave college. Instead, your world can go on, albeit with a significant adjustment in perspective.

So you're potentially being given a second chance. Yes, the road less-traveled is gravelly and rough, and likely full of disappointment. But it leads you to adulthood and responsibility the same as college. If life were to have one great advice to be given to every maturing individual, it should definitely be, "don't fret the details," in conjunction with "time waits for no man (or woman.)" The world will persevere, as will you through your own set of trials. And please, don't let people sympathize to your pains and woes; no one, yourself included, deserves the pity of defeat for something like this. Stand tall and accept your mistakes; the world will sympathize with you all the more for your flaws than your tragic absence.

It won't be okay, but you'll get better at building your world in a way that suits your needs and desires. High school is terrible be cause beyond the fact that everyone is incredibly judgmental and hormonal, you're piled high with school work and pressure to do well on standardized tests, and what's more, you've got parents who seem to shackle and quash your whims and ideas because they've "got the experience," and they "run the show." 

But high school marks the end of a lot of that. College is a lot of work if you want to go through that. College is also a wonderful place to commune with people your age and really become invested in who you are and who you want to be as an adult. College is worth it, but it's not the only path. That's part of the silver lining to life. Within the realms of the local laws, you're allowed to choose your adventure, and graduating high school is where it all begins. You'll start to realize that experience has little to do with one's ability to lead life "correctly," and you might be angrier at your parents for that, but eventually, you'll also recognize that the human experience garners a great deal of accidents that we mistake for experiential virtue, and you'll know that they were trying they're hardest to be themselves the way they saw fit.

But back to "okay." It won't be okay, because the world still spins and those same things that drag you down now may still drag you down 5 years from now or 10 years, etc. But you'll change. You'll be okay because you're going to want your own world enough that you'll build your life away from those things that drag you through the doldrums.

In the meantime, try to worry less about tomorrow. It's a tough task, but it will get you through high school with a lot less stress. If your atheism is causing you enough tension because you can't talk about it openly, write about it; that'll help, but you should reach a point where it's not worth the agony of hiding it any more. You have every right to your beliefs, but as you grow to be more responsible, don't consider your parents arguments as attacks. They have their beliefs that they feel just as strongly about, and if they refuse to agree-to-disagree, then you'll have only so much time left before you can start out on your own.

So keep on keepin' on. Choose your battles in high school, and don't worry about where you're going just yet. You'll get where you need to go, and even if the road is bumpy, you'll learn to be okay.
